title: CFO Quarterly Close — Q2: Tightening the Screws
subtitle: Six harder weeks: tighter covenant, bigger surprises, less margin for error
theme: First-time CFO heads into Q2 with a covenant the lenders just re-cut, an audit finding that didn't fully die, an unsolicited M&A approach, and an analyst day on the calendar
description: Q1 bought you credibility. Q2 spends it. The lender's new term sheet shaves $3M off your covenant headroom; the auditor flagged a revenue-cut-off issue that needs final remediation; a strategic acquirer slid an unsolicited LOI under the door; the CEO wants you on the analyst day stage. Six rounds, every one a real choice with real second-order consequences. Built as the canonical follow-on to the Q1 simulation.
learning_objectives: Negotiate a covenant amendment without pretending the business is what it isn't
Close out an audit finding cleanly — including how to brief the audit committee chair
Evaluate an unsolicited M&A approach with discipline, including when to say no fast
Run an analyst day where bad news is delivered first and well
Decide between a debt raise, a structured equity raise, and a cost reset
Sequence year-end close so controls survive contact with growth

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are the CFO of a $90M ARR Series-D fintech, eight months into the seat
Each round is one week's executive decision; the consequences accumulate
Your choices move six dimensions: commercial acumen, governance, controllership, cash discipline, decision quality, executive communication
Stakes are higher than Q1 — covenant headroom is half what it was, and the board now has an activist-leaning independent
tips: Speed of honest signal beats polished delay
Boards forgive misses; they don't forgive surprises
An unsolicited LOI is a gift only if you have the discipline to refuse it

target_audience: MBA students, finance professionals, aspiring CFOs

difficulty_curve.description: R14 — adaptive ramp so MBA students who skipped Q1 aren't crushed in W14. Tutorial scaffolds the lender meeting; core is the operating quarter; mastery is analyst day + year-end close.

soundscape.description: R15 — boardroom ambience for the CFO Q2 sim. Royalty-free CC0 loops served from /assets/audio/.

hi._meta: R17 — Hindi translation of CFO Q2. Frontend uses these strings when locale === 'hi'.
hi.title: सीएफओ तिमाही समापन — Q2: दबाव बढ़ता हुआ
hi.subtitle: छह कठिन सप्ताह: सख्त कोवेनेंट, बड़े आश्चर्य, गलती की कम गुंजाइश
hi.theme: पहली बार के सीएफओ Q2 में प्रवेश कर रहे हैं — एक नया कोवेनेंट, ऑडिट का अधूरा निष्कर्ष, बिन माँगा एम&ए प्रस्ताव, और एक एनालिस्ट डे सामने है
hi.description: Q1 ने आपकी विश्वसनीयता बनाई। Q2 उसे खर्च करता है। ऋणदाता की नई शर्त आपके कोवेनेंट हेडरूम से $3M काट देती है; ऑडिटर ने राजस्व कट-ऑफ की एक चेतावनी छोड़ी है जिसका समाधान बाकी है; एक रणनीतिक अधिग्रहणकर्ता ने अनुरोधित LOI भेजा है; CEO चाहते हैं कि आप एनालिस्ट डे के मंच पर हों। छह राउंड, हर एक वास्तविक निर्णय और वास्तविक दूसरी-स्तर के परिणाम।
learning_objectives: व्यापार की वास्तविकता को छुपाए बिना कोवेनेंट संशोधन पर बातचीत करना
ऑडिट निष्कर्ष को साफ-सुथरे ढंग से बंद करना — ऑडिट कमिटी चेयर को ब्रीफ करने सहित
एक बिन माँगे एम&ए प्रस्ताव का अनुशासित मूल्यांकन — और जरूरत हो तो जल्दी 'नहीं' कहना
एनालिस्ट डे चलाना जहाँ बुरी ख़बर पहले और अच्छी तरह दी जाती है
ऋण, संरचित इक्विटी, या लागत-रीसेट के बीच चुनाव करना
वर्ष के अंत के समापन को इस तरह क्रमबद्ध करना कि नियंत्रण विकास के साथ टिके

how_to_play.title: खेल कैसे खेलें
steps: आप एक $90M ARR सीरीज़-D फ़िनटेक के सीएफओ हैं, इस भूमिका में आठ महीने पूरे कर चुके हैं
हर राउंड एक सप्ताह का एग्ज़िक्यूटिव निर्णय है; परिणाम जुड़ते जाते हैं
आपके निर्णय छह आयामों को प्रभावित करते हैं: कमर्शियल समझ, गवर्नेंस, कंट्रोलरशिप, कैश अनुशासन, निर्णय गुणवत्ता, संप्रेषण
Q1 की तुलना में दांव अधिक हैं — कोवेनेंट हेडरूम आधा है, और बोर्ड में अब एक एक्टिविस्ट-झुकाव वाला स्वतंत्र निदेशक है
tips: ईमानदार संकेत की गति, चमकदार देरी से बेहतर है
बोर्ड चूक माफ़ करते हैं; आश्चर्य माफ़ नहीं करते
एक बिन माँगा LOI तभी उपहार है जब आपके पास उसे अस्वीकार करने का अनुशासन हो

core_skills.name: कमर्शियल समझ
core_skills.description: P&L, इकाई अर्थशास्त्र, मूल्य निर्धारण को एक सुसंगत कहानी के रूप में पढ़ना।

core_skills.name: गवर्नेंस निर्णय
core_skills.description: बोर्ड तैयारी, ऑडिट कमिटी, संचालन बनाम बोर्ड स्तर का अंतर।

core_skills.name: कंट्रोलरशिप
core_skills.description: क्लोज़ अनुशासन, एक्रुअल्स, नियंत्रण, ऑडिट तैयारी।

core_skills.name: एग्ज़िक्यूटिव संप्रेषण
core_skills.description: बोर्ड और एनालिस्ट को बुरी ख़बर पहले देना; गति बनाम पॉलिश।

w14_covenant_amend.title: सप्ताह 14 — ऋणदाता ने कोवेनेंट दोबारा काटा
w14_covenant_amend.scenario: आपके ऋणदाता, ब्याज दर के माहौल का हवाला देते हुए, एक मसौदा संशोधन भेजते हैं: न्यूनतम कैश कोवेनेंट $25M से $28M, MFN क्लॉज़ जोड़ा गया, और 0.5% शुल्क। हेडरूम $17M से $10M पर एक रात में गिर जाता है। CEO ज़ोर से धकेलना चाहते हैं। ट्रेज़री सोचता है तेज़ी से हस्ताक्षर रिश्ता बचाएगा।

w16_audit_finding.title: सप्ताह 16 — ऑडिट निष्कर्ष जो मरा नहीं
w16_audit_finding.scenario: Q1 ऑडिट राजस्व कट-ऑफ पर 'महत्वपूर्ण कमी' (मटीरियल वीकनेस नहीं) के साथ बंद हुआ। ऑडिट कमिटी चेयर पूछती हैं कि क्या आपके द्वारा प्रस्तुत उपचार योजना वास्तव में निष्पादित हो रही है — कंट्रोलर कहते हैं तीन महीने बाद भी 70% आइटम 'प्रगति में' हैं। SOX समय-सीमा कड़ी है।

w18_unsolicited_loi.title: सप्ताह 18 — एक अनुरोध-रहित LOI
w18_unsolicited_loi.scenario: एक रणनीतिक अधिग्रहणकर्ता (एक $4B सार्वजनिक-सूचीबद्ध समकक्ष) सीधे CEO को एक अनुरोध-रहित LOI ईमेल करता है: $850M नकद + स्टॉक, 60 दिनों में डायलिजेंस पूरा होने के साथ। उनका सार्वजनिक मल्टीपल 5x ARR है; हमारा, निजी तुलनात्मकों पर, 7x है। CEO उत्साहित हैं। बोर्ड को 72 घंटे में आपकी राय चाहिए।

w20_capital_decision.title: सप्ताह 20 — पूँजी का निर्णय
w20_capital_decision.scenario: वर्तमान बर्न पर 14 महीने रनवे और विकास फिर से तेज़ी पकड़ रहा है, CEO जुटाना चाहते हैं। मेज पर तीन विकल्प: (1) $1.1B पोस्ट पर $80M सीरीज़ E; (2) SOFR+650 पर $50M स्ट्रक्चर्ड डेट विद वारंट कवरेज; (3) लागत-रीसेट — बर्न $3.2M से $2.4M पर लाएँ, जुटान 6 महीने आगे धकेलें। बाज़ार उतार-चढ़ाव में है।

w22_analyst_day.title: सप्ताह 22 — एनालिस्ट डे का मंच
w22_analyst_day.scenario: इन्वेस्टर डे दो सप्ताह में। CEO चाहते हैं 4-वर्षीय ARR योजना ($90M → $300M), ग्रॉस मार्जिन ट्रेजेक्टरी, और FCF इन्फ़्लेक्शन। मार्केटिंग ने स्लाइड बनाई हैं जो चार साल तक 50% Y/Y दिखाती हैं। आपका मॉडल कहता है 40%, 35%, 30%, 25%। मंच के बाद तीन सेल-साइड एनालिस्ट 1:1 के लिए निर्धारित हैं।

w24_yearend_close.title: सप्ताह 24 — वर्षांत समापन
w24_yearend_close.scenario: अंतिम क्लोज़। दो खुले आइटम: (1) राजस्व कट-ऑफ का मुद्दा एक $4.2M डील पर फिर उभरता है जिसे 31 दिसंबर तक अर्जित नहीं माना जा सकता, (2) सेल्स ने $9M प्री-पे बुक किया है जिसे लीगल ने संभावित रूप से वापसी-योग्य बताया है। ऑडिटर कमरे में हैं। यदि आप कॉल आक्रामक तरीके से लें तो Q4 संख्याएँ योजना से 1.5% ऊपर हैं, रूढ़िवादी कॉल पर 0.5% नीचे।

psychological_framework.description: CFO dimensions: commercial acumen, governance judgment, controllership, cash discipline, decision quality, communication.

core_skills.name: Commercial Acumen
core_skills.description: Reading P&L, unit economics, pricing as a coherent story.

core_skills.name: Governance Judgment
core_skills.description: Board prep, audit committee, separation of operating vs board-level.

core_skills.name: Controllership
core_skills.description: Close discipline, accruals, controls, audit readiness.

core_skills.name: Decision Quality
core_skills.description: Calibrated forecasts; reversibility; pre-mortems on numbers.

core_skills.name: Executive Communication
core_skills.description: Owning the narrative on misses; analyst-call discipline.

llm_config.audience_default: First-time CFO of a $90M ARR Series-D fintech, two quarters into the seat

coaching_moment: Q2 isn't Q1 again. The lender, the audit committee, and the analyst desk all remember Q1 — your credibility now compounds either way.

rounds.title: Week 14 — The Lender Re-Cuts the Covenant
rounds.scenario: Your lender, citing rate environment, sends a draft amendment: minimum cash covenant moves from $25M to $28M, MFN clause added, and a 0.5% fee. Headroom drops from $17M to $10M overnight. The CEO wants to push back hard. Treasury thinks signing fast keeps the relationship.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: CFO and treasurer reviewing a covenant amendment letter, tense, semi-realistic boardroom

choices.label: Counter with a 13-week cash model showing $32M floor; ask for $26M covenant + drop the MFN; sign within 5 days
choices.feedback: You traded speed for a defensible counter and won 3 of 3 asks. Lender respect, board respect, headroom intact.
choices.expert_rationale: A 13-week cash model is the only currency lenders trust. You bought $6M of headroom for the cost of one weekend.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Treasury's instinct to sign fast was right about the relationship and wrong about the math — the MFN compounds every future amendment.

choices.label: Sign as drafted to keep the relationship; document concerns in board minutes
choices.feedback: Relationship preserved. Headroom now $10M. Audit committee asks why no counter.
choices.expert_rationale: Documenting concerns in minutes is cosmetic if you didn't fight for the number — the minutes will read as alibi, not analysis.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You preserved the relationship and lost the negotiation. Lenders read 'sign clean' as 'no leverage' — and price the next amendment accordingly.

choices.label: Reject the amendment publicly — leak intent to bank competitors to force a re-bid
choices.feedback: Two banks bid; existing lender pulls first draft and re-prices at +75 bps. Net worse.
choices.expert_rationale: Public escalation in lender disputes is a one-shot tool — and you're not yet the CFO who has earned the right to use it.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimised for posture and inherited the worst pricing in the room. Lenders talk to each other faster than you think.

rounds.title: Week 16 — The Audit Finding That Wouldn't Die
rounds.scenario: Q1 audit closed with a 'significant deficiency' (not material weakness) on revenue cut-off. The audit committee chair asks whether the remediation plan you submitted is actually being executed — Controller says 70% of items are still 'in progress' three months later. SOX timeline is tight.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: CFO walking auditor through revenue cut-off remediation, semi-realistic conference room

choices.label: Take personal ownership: weekly tracker, name a remediation owner per item, brief the chair before next AC meeting
choices.feedback: AC chair gives you direct line. 'Significant deficiency' clears in next quarter's audit. CEO trust grows.
choices.expert_rationale: Audit findings die only when the CFO owns them at the desk-level for one quarter. Delegation is the failure mode.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Delegating remediation tracking is what got you here. The fix is unglamorous: you in the weekly meeting until the items close.

choices.label: Push it back to Controller with a 30-day deadline; you focus on the covenant work
choices.feedback: Controller misses the deadline. AC chair raises it directly to the board. You lose the next round of trust.
choices.expert_rationale: Audit committees read CFO delegation on findings as CFO disengagement on controls.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Controllers don't fail because they're under-skilled — they fail because the CFO didn't make the timeline a CFO timeline.

choices.label: Hire a Big-4 advisory team to remediate at $400K; fastest path to closure
choices.feedback: Items close on time. Audit committee asks why an internal control needed external hands. Cost flagged in MD&A.
choices.expert_rationale: Outsourced remediation closes findings; it doesn't close the underlying weakness in your team.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: $400K bought you the calendar and not the capability — and the audit committee can read the difference in a footnote.

rounds.title: Week 18 — An Unsolicited LOI
rounds.scenario: A strategic acquirer (a $4B publicly-listed peer) emails the CEO directly with an unsolicited LOI: $850M cash + stock, with diligence completing in 60 days. Their public multiple is 5x ARR; ours, on private comparables, is 7x. CEO is excited. The board wants your read in 72 hours.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: CFO at desk reading an unsolicited LOI letter, weighing options, semi-realistic

choices.label: Recommend a fast, written decline citing valuation gap and 24-month plan; offer to host them as a customer instead
choices.feedback: Board respects the discipline. Acquirer raises bid by 15% three weeks later; you have a real number to negotiate from.
choices.expert_rationale: The first unsolicited offer is the floor, never the ceiling. Saying no fast and writing it down protects the floor.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Most first-time CFOs treat an LOI as flattery. It's a price discovery instrument the acquirer is using on you, not for you.

choices.label: Open a data room, run 60-day diligence; you can always say no later
choices.feedback: Diligence consumes 40% of finance team for 8 weeks. Q2 close slips. You walk away with no deal and a tired team.
choices.expert_rationale: A data room is never neutral — it's a commitment device the acquirer uses on your team's calendar.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'You can always say no later' is true and irrelevant — by then you've spent the team's quarter.

choices.label: Counter at $1.4B with a 30-day exclusivity window; force them to put a real number on the table
choices.feedback: Acquirer walks. Word spreads in the corridor that you 'shopped' the company. Two enterprise customers ask the CEO if you're for sale.
choices.expert_rationale: Aggressive counters on unsolicited LOIs only work when you have a real auction to fall back on — you don't.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You priced the company before you priced the rumor cost. The rumor compounds even when the deal dies.

rounds.title: Week 20 — The Capital Decision
rounds.scenario: With 14 months runway at current burn and growth re-accelerating, the CEO wants to raise. Three options on the table: (1) $80M Series E at $1.1B post; (2) $50M structured debt at SOFR+650 with warrant coverage; (3) cost reset — pull burn from $3.2M to $2.4M, push raise 6 months. Markets are choppy.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: CFO at whiteboard sketching three capital paths, semi-realistic, evening light

choices.label: Series E now at $1.1B post — bank the capital while it's available, plan from strength
choices.feedback: Capital banked. You diluted 7%. Two quarters later valuations climb 30% — board asks about timing.
choices.expert_rationale: Raising into uncertainty is rarely wrong; it's just rarely optimised.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You bought certainty at the price of upside. Board hindsight is unfair but it's still the room you brief next quarter.

choices.label: $50M structured debt with warrants — minimal dilution, accept the higher cost of capital
choices.feedback: Debt closes in 6 weeks. Warrants represent 1.2% dilution. Runway extends to 22 months. Board approves unanimously.
choices.expert_rationale: Structured debt at this stage is the best dilution-vs-runway trade if your cash discipline can defend the covenants.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Equity-first is the default for a reason — but at 14 months runway with a working covenant, debt is the discipline-rewarding move.

choices.label: Cost reset — RIF, push the raise 6 months, target growth re-acceleration before the next round
choices.feedback: Burn drops to $2.4M. Three senior engineering leaders leave within 90 days. Q3 product velocity slips. Growth flatlines.
choices.expert_rationale: Cost resets work only when the next 12 months don't need execution velocity — almost never the case at $90M ARR growing.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: RIFs solve cash and break compounding. The team you cut is the team that was about to deliver.

rounds.title: Week 22 — Analyst Day Stage
rounds.scenario: Investor day in two weeks. CEO wants 4-year ARR plan ($90M → $300M), gross margin trajectory, and FCF inflection. Marketing has drafted slides showing 50% Y/Y for four years. Your model says 40%, 35%, 30%, 25%. Three sell-side analysts are scheduled for 1:1s after stage.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: CFO on analyst day stage, slide deck visible, audience in dark theatre, semi-realistic
rounds.reflection_prompt: Analyst-day guidance is a contract analysts will quote back to you for two years. What does it cost you when the headline you publish is the one your own model can't defend?

choices.label: Publish your model: 40/35/30/25 with explicit drivers; CEO presents the strategy, you present the numbers
choices.feedback: Two analysts upgrade citing 'finance discipline.' Stock sells off 4% on the day; recovers and runs +12% over next quarter on credibility.
choices.expert_rationale: Calibrated guidance compounds; aspirational guidance gets re-cut once and never trusted again.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Analyst-day guidance is the one piece of paper analysts will quote back to you for years. Make it the one you can defend.

choices.label: Publish marketing's 50/50/50/50 plan; explain that finance's model is 'conservative scenario'
choices.feedback: Stock pops 8% on the day. Q3 misses the 50% marker. Stock drops 22%. Two analysts go to neutral.
choices.expert_rationale: There is no such thing as a 'conservative scenario' on stage — analysts model the headline number.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You bought one good day and three bad quarters. The headline is the contract.

choices.label: Give 1-year guidance only; refuse to publish a 4-year plan
choices.feedback: Analysts mark you down for 'lack of vision.' Multiple compresses 0.8x relative to peers. Stock flat for two quarters.
choices.expert_rationale: At Series-D scale, refusing a long-term plan is a tax — analysts price ambiguity at a discount.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Hiding behind 'we don't guide long-term' costs you the multiple. The plan is going to exist in their model anyway.

rounds.title: Week 24 — Year-End Close
rounds.scenario: Final close. Two open items: (1) revenue cut-off issue resurfaces on a $4.2M deal that may not have been earned by Dec 31, (2) sales has booked a $9M pre-pay that legal flagged as potentially refundable. Auditors are in the room. Q4 numbers are 1.5% above plan if you take the calls aggressively, 0.5% below if you call them conservatively.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: CFO walking auditors through year-end close, calendar Dec 31 visible, semi-realistic
rounds.reflection_prompt: Year-end is the one close where the line between CFO and controller is whether you can say 'no' to a number you'd love to take. What does that 'no' cost in this close — and what does the 'yes' cost two quarters from now?

choices.label: Defer the $4.2M; classify $9M as deferred revenue; report 0.5% below plan with full disclosure
choices.feedback: Auditors sign. Audit committee notes 'high-quality close.' Stock dips 2% on the miss; recovers as analysts cite controls.
choices.expert_rationale: Year-end is the one close where the difference between a CFO and a controller is whether you can say 'no' to a number you'd love to take.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Aggressive calls at year-end always have a half-life — they show up as restatement risk in next year's 10-K.

choices.label: Take the $4.2M (defensible technical position); defer the $9M; report 0.5% above plan
choices.feedback: Auditors push back hard on the $4.2M; close slips 4 days; technical adjustment in February reverses the gain. Audit fee +$200K.
choices.expert_rationale: 'Defensible' technical positions at year-end cost more than they're worth — the audit fee alone usually erases the headline gain.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Splitting the difference at year-end is the worst of both worlds: you took the audit pain and didn't take the headline.

choices.label: Take both: classify $9M as recognised; report 1.5% above plan
choices.feedback: Auditors flag material weakness on the $9M. Q1 next year requires restatement. Two board members ask whether you should remain CFO.
choices.expert_rationale: There is no version of CFO career where year-end aggressive calls survive the next audit.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: This is the one round where the upside is one quarter and the downside is your entire seat.

challenge_persona_ladder: your audit committee chair — soft-spoken, asks one good question per round and listens to the answer with full attention
an activist-leaning independent director — quoting your own forecasts back at you and pressing on the assumption you skipped
a sell-side analyst from a hedge-fund-backed desk — direct, numbers-only, looking for the gap between your guidance and your model

hallmarks: Owned the lender narrative with a 13-week cash model rather than relationship preservation
Personally drove audit-finding remediation rather than delegating to Controller
Declined the unsolicited LOI cleanly, raising the floor for any future bid
Chose structured debt over equity dilution and over a cost reset
Published calibrated 4-year guidance and accepted the day-one stock pain
Closed year-end conservatively with full disclosure rather than chasing the headline
Signed the covenant amendment without a counter, surrendering $6M of headroom
Delegated audit remediation and watched it slip into next quarter's audit
Opened a data room on an unsolicited LOI and lost a quarter of finance bandwidth
Took the marketing-friendly long-range plan and missed the headline two quarters later
Took aggressive year-end calls that the auditor reversed in February

glossary_terms.definition: A formal change to the financial covenants in a loan agreement, typically negotiated when the borrower is approaching breach or the lender wants to re-price the relationship.
An audit finding less severe than a material weakness but still requiring board reporting; indicates a control gap that could allow misstatement.
A non-binding letter of intent from a potential acquirer not invited by a formal sale process; usually a price-discovery move and rarely the final number.
Debt with non-standard features such as warrants, payment-in-kind interest, or revenue-share, used when senior debt is unavailable but full-equity dilution is undesirable.
Forward financial projections published with explicit assumptions and conservative bias, designed to be defensible across multiple quarters rather than impressive on day one.
The accounting determination of which fiscal period a revenue-generating transaction belongs to; a frequent audit issue at year-end when contracts straddle period boundaries.
